before: Can guile contain the 'character of the subsistence'? Who can grasp with their hands the one 'who carries all things by the word of his own power'? 'I am Jesus whom you persecute' (Acts 9:5). I keep you as a bridegroom for my bride.
Why do you persecute that which you are about to be persecuted for a little later? Instead, you wear out your feet in vain; you sweat uselessly and toil excessively.
The one being persecuted by you sits in the bosom of the Father.
'I am Jesus whom you persecute' (Acts 22:10), not realizing that he is being driven toward his own struggle.

Why do you fight against the wise one? You aim arrows at a benefactor unlike any other, a nourisher whom you suckle, through whom the earth sets the table for you without care for the fruits. You slander the Savior; if he were to tighten his hand, who would free you from sins, who would release you from your bonds, and from whom would you find the deed? Thus, this Paul—who was once a persecutor and is now an evangelist, once a pirate and now a pilot, once a wolf and now a shepherd, once lead and now gold, once a blasphemer and now one spoken well of by all—this man is a beginner among teachers, exceptional among those who bear God, great among prophets, wiser among apostles, unhurt among athletes, more glorious among the heralds of the truth, and more powerful among the soldiers of piety.

For who was 'flogged three times' and a fourth? Who, as that man boasts, 'received one hundred and ninety-nine from the Jews' (2 Corinthians 11:24; John 21:25)? Who, having made a shipwreck in the deep by night instead of a bridal bath, and having made 'many journeys' profitable—each one highly profitable? Who faced the dangers of robbers, the dangers of kin, the dangers of rivers, the dangers in the wilderness, the dangers from nations, and the dangers among false brothers, yet did not scatter his wealth through endurance? Who of all the churches carries the burden of care, yet manages the experience of cargoes without being constrained, without weighing down his shoulders, and without bending his neck? Who then abhors sin so intensely, yet possesses such compassion for sinners? No one.
For he always strives that we might attain the eternal good things in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages of the ages.
Amen.

before: An encomium by Hesychius, a presbyter of Jerusalem, to the holy apostles Peter and Paul.
The rose is indeed beautiful, becoming fragrant when the season of spring offers it; yet if it is joined with the lily, it rightly becomes even more fragrant.
For myrrh is indeed mixed with myrrh, resulting in a double enjoyment of the fragrance found here.
Peter is splendid in himself, and among the splendid ones he is most radiant.
He is the crown of the apostolic fellowship, the eye of discipleship, and the very countenance of zeal and faith.
He is the trumpet of the mystery, a tongue that taught many tongues; he is an unblamable shepherd and a sleepless helmsman, an unerring charioteer.
He is like a pharmacist who has prepared the medicinal remedy of repentance.

He is a fisherman of the sea, through whom fish are caught even into heaven—his net, made of linen, catches wonders; the bait is the sufferings, the hook is the cross, and the fold is the resurrection.
He is the keeper of the treasury, in whom the Father holds the treasures, the Son holds the bridal chambers, the Spirit holds the table, and the angels hold the dances.
But with Paul added, the wall becomes doubled and cannot be captured.
The spring becomes two-mouthed, unceasingly watering the whole earth, and the lake becomes two-faced, so that every vessel sailing along its banks is saved.
The quail speaks with the swallow, the dove utters sound with the turtle-dove, and the aulos and the syrinx together play a holy and sweet melody.
"A youth with a saint, and straight is the way" is their path, just as the wise man proclaimed in Proverbs (Proverbs 22:6).
The lamb and the wolf graze together, the shepherd is glorified, and the wonders of the one made paradoxical are revealed.
A bull and a lion graze together in a single pasture, and the one who strengthened the bull and tamed the lion enjoys the resulting praises.

Was not Paul a lion when he was still Saul? For while he was slaughtering the flock, he scattered them, striking terror into the shepherds; he roared within Jerusalem, flew through the cities, and stirred the marketplaces into uproar.

He sought to make even the villages uninhabited, and he did not cease dragging men into prison and women into bonds; yet he was defeated by the endurance of men and was weaker than the courage of women.
He ran in vain, for he was not following the way; he was beating the air in vain, yet he was not sufficient to find his adversary.
Christ, therefore, being wise himself and having passed by as a good man, has made use of meekness; by leaving behind the high things, he promotes the humble.
He did not kindle a fire, nor did he stir up storms, nor did he shake the foundations of the mountains.
He did not wield an angelic, wide-mouthed sword, but is called by a gentle voice and as a lover of mankind: "Saul, Saul," he says, "why do you persecute me?" (Acts 9:4)
What wealth of yours did I take away? In what glory did I strip you?
